newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS-Dlr/mark volatilities sag as spot retreats.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS-Dlr/mark volatilities sag as spot retreats.

text.p: Implied volatilities for shorter-dated dollar/mark options sagged in lackluster U.S. trading as the spot greenback retreated from Monday's 37-month highs, dealers said.
The dollar's decline was widely viewed as a short-term correction in an overall uptrend and did not fuel concern about the downside risk, they added.
"It's been a pretty orderly move down," said a trader at a U.S. bank in New York.
Traders noted that back-end volatilities were holding in relatively well.

"I think the front-end is just taking a breather after the G7 (Group of Seven meeting on Sunday) for a couple of days," said a bank trader in Toronto. "People are getting out of longs (in shorter maturities), but longer term they still think we're going to see some volatility in the market."
The dollar/mark volatility curve steepened slightly, with one-month losing a quarter point from Monday to 8.4/8.6 percent and one-year shedding about 0.1 to 9.0/9.2 percent.
However, Friday expiries were steady at 8.0/10.0 percent, compared with 7.5/8.5 for a standard full week, due to Friday's April U.S. employment report.

The Toronto trader said volatilities for very short maturities could pop up just before Friday when demand for gamma, which provides quick premium acceleration, starts to outweigh time-decay concerns.
Sterling volatilities were firm as the market awaited Thursday's U.K. general elections. One-month cable rose 0.2 point to 7.3/7.6 percent, while one-week blipped up half a point to 7.8/8.8.
The pound rallied against the dollar in early trade, helping traders justify the rich premiums. Spot cable rose to highs above $1.6320 from earlier lows near $1.6220.

Dollar/yen volatilities were steady to softer. They were holding in better than dollar/mark only because they had already been deflated on Monday after an initial spike up following Sunday's G7 meeting, traders said.
One-month dollar/yen stood at 8.3/8.6 percent at U.S. midsession, virtually unchanged from late Monday levels.

Demand for yen calls was drying up as the G7 meeting did not yield any strong statement to contain the dollar's strength against the yen, traders said. Risk reversals, the cost of swapping equally out-of-the-money puts and calls, were at around par across the maturity curve.
Until Monday, shorter-dated risk reversals had been slightly skewed for yen calls.

The Golden Week holidays in Japan, which kicked off today, could be subduing interest in dollar/yen, although this year's Golden Week was less significant than usual because of the overlap with the weekend, traders said.
